       used for hyperspectral image classiﬁcation. Though this variation of CNNs brings

        notable beneﬁts in capturing joint spectral and spatial features, they suffer fromC
poor computational efﬁciency, causing low training/inference speed of the model. On the

 contrary, CNN-based methods with 1D and 2D kernels are efﬁcient, but mostly restricted

 to extract either spectral or spatial feature. Moreover, most CNN based hyperspectral

image classiﬁcation frameworks are incapable of simultaneously taking advantages of

residual and dense aggregation without over-allocating parameters or information loss

 for feature re-usage. This chapter presents a novel attention-based lattice network (ALN)

 to overcome these shortcomings and investigate its capability for hyperspectral image

 classiﬁcation. The proposed framework can effectively harness the advantages of residual

and dense aggregations to achieve outstanding accuracy performance and computational

 efﬁciency, simultaneously. The proposed method employs a unique joint spectral-spatial

attention mechanism to capture both spectral and spatial information effectively. Our

extensive experimental investigation veriﬁes the effectiveness and efﬁciency of the ALN

architecture for hyperspectral image classiﬁcation. Quantitative measurements and

visual results of generated classiﬁcation maps demonstrate that ALN achieves superior

performance and efﬁciency against state-of-the-art deep learning benchmark approaches.

IMAGE CLASSIFICATION

5.1  Introduction


Hyperspectral image (HSI) analysis plays a fundamental role in a wide range of remote

sensing applications such as environmental management [97] and agriculture [36, 62].

HSIs are captured from hyperspectral sensors and consist of many narrow spectral bands

that carry detailed spectral and spatial information of the observed objects. With the

capability to support discriminative spectral and spatial features analysis makes HSI a

favourable choice of precise identiﬁcation and characterization of the physical, chemical

and material properties of the areas of interest.

   However, the extensive number of spectral bands may cause feature redundancy and

the curse of dimensionality problems [41]. Much effort has been made in the literature

to alleviate the challenges using band selection or feature extraction approaches [79,

103, 114]. In addition to spectral information, as there is spatial consistency in the

hyperspectral image, i.e. pixels within an adjacent spatial area tend to have the same

class label, exploiting spatial correlation has also been studied. In this regard, methods

like sparse representation [49, 89], and superpixel-based approaches [84, 85] have

taken advantage of spatial information to enhance hyperspectral image classiﬁcation

performance. Moreover, as taking advantage of both spectral and spatial information

together are desirable, methods including 3D local binary pattern (LBP) [86], and 3D

Gabor wavelet transformation [87] are applied to exploit spatial-spectral characteristics

of hyperspectral images.

   The traditional approaches rely on handcrafted features and cannot effectively extract

discriminative features for robust HSI classiﬁcation. On the other hand, convolutional

neural networks (CNNs) have shown outstanding performance on many computer vision

and image processing tasks [60]. Inspired by the biological process of the visual system,

they produce discriminative and representative features from raw input signals without

any prior manipulation. Thus, CNNs effectively address the limitation of conventional

HSI classiﬁcation methods. They deploy a uniﬁed end-to-end learning-based framework

to optimize feature extraction tasks as well as classiﬁcation tasks simultaneously. In

particular, residual networks [67] and densely connected convolutional networks [77]

are two major advances to facilitate information circulation and the ability to explore

effective new features. Various 1D and 2D CNN based methods are adopted to extract

the spectral and/or spatial features, respectively. For instance, Hu et al. [74] developed

a deep convolutional network that employs 1D convolution functions to exploit the

spectral feature of each pixel’s spectrum. In [201] a uniﬁed framework is proposed which


                                   64

5.1. INTRODUCTION



integrates 2D CNN and RNN to acquire both spectral and spatial information. Besides,

many recent CNN-based methods employ 3D convolutional kernels to exploit both spatial

and spectral information at the same time [25, 63, 68, 222], so that rich spectral-spatial

co-related features can be generated for hyperspectral image classiﬁcation.

   Despite the signiﬁcant improvement of different CNN-based frameworks over tradi-

tional approaches for HSI classiﬁcation, they suffer from several shortcomings. First, 1D

CNNs and 2D CNNs are not capable of considering both spectral and spatial properties

and are limited to either spectral-based or spatial-based classiﬁcation [63, 105]. 3D-CNNs

can address this drawback, however, with an expensive computational overhead [64].

Second, due to the small training sample issue of HSI datasets, many existing CNN-

based HSI classiﬁcation methods cannot effectively and yet efﬁciently take advantages

of residual [67] and/or dense [77] information aggregation advances so that they may be

threatened by overﬁtting issue and lack of good generalization capability.

   Recently, we [127] proposed a method to estimate the clean speech magnitude, which

is corrupted by different noise levels. This method used a residual-dense lattice (RDL)

topology to exploit the advantages of both residual and dense aggregations without over-

allocating parameters for feature re-usage [224]. This deep lattice framework showed

the state-of-the-art performance in enhancing sequential signals, e.g. speech. However,

most of the existing CNN based HSI methods are not able to take advantage of both

residual and dense aggregation types efﬁciently.

   In this chapter, we introduce a new network structure to fully exploit the potential

of lattice topology for addressing the aforementioned shortcomings of CNN based HSI

classiﬁcation methods. To this end, ﬁrst, we adopt a unique lattice network of 2D

convolutional kernels which provides a lightweight model empowered by both residual

and dense aggregation links. A two-step bottleneck technique is also incorporated with

each convolutional elements to make the lattice framework more efﬁcient. We further

incorporate lightweight and yet effective spectral and spatial attention mechanisms to

the proposed HSI classiﬁcation framework to effectively exploit information carried by

inter-dependencies among spectral bands and spatial features. We refer to our framework

as attention-based lattice network (ALN), whose overview is illustrated in Figure 5.1.

   The main contribution of our work is summarized as follows.


   1. First, the proposed 2D convolutional residual-dense lattice can provide a lightweight

     framework to address the small training sample set issue in remote sensing HSI

      classiﬁcation and maintain the efﬁciency of the ALN model in terms of computation

      cost and time.

   2. Second, the proposed two-stage attention strategy ensures the joint spectral-spatial

      features are exploited throughout the network. In particular, the ﬁrst stage of

   3. Third, extensive experiments show that the new ALN can produce higher HSI

      classiﬁcation performance than several benchmark CNN based HSI classiﬁcation

     methods without sacriﬁcing efﬁciency in speed, model size and computational cost.

      Further, extensive ablation analyses are conducted to investigate the role of every

     component of the proposed network.


   The rest of this article is organized as follows. Section 5.2 brieﬂy reviews related

5.2  Related Works


5.2.1  Deep Learning for Hyperspectral Image Classiﬁcation

In the past few years, signiﬁcant progress has been made for hyperspectral image classi-

ﬁcation by developing discriminative learning-based methods using deep convolutional

neural networks (CNNs). Generally, CNN-based HSI classiﬁcation methods are cate-


                                   66

5.2. RELATED WORKS



gorised into three main groups: spectral CNNs, spatial CNNs and spectral-spatial CNNs.

While the ﬁrst group focuses on extracting spectral information for each pixel in hy-

perspectral images, the second group relies on extracting spatial correlation of pixels

within a spatial region. The third group of CNN-based HSI classiﬁcation methods aim at

integrating both spectral and spatial features simultaneously. Since each spatial pixel in

the hyperspectral image corresponds to a spectral vector with hundreds of bands, 1D

CNN-based methods are widely used to exploit a deep feature of the spectrum [74]. In ad-

dition to popular 1D CNN frameworks, 1D generative adversarial networks (GANs) [223]

are also applied to extract spectral information.

   With respect to the spatial-based classiﬁcation approaches, 2D CNNs are the most

common methods used for RGB image analysis and recognition tasks. Chen et al. [27]

proposed the very ﬁrst 2D CNN model, which extracts deep features from the latent

space of a stacked autoencoder framework to classify hyperspectral data. Likewise, a

stacked sparse autoencoder (SSAE) [221] was introduced to exploit a multiscale sparse

deep spatial feature representation for HSI classiﬁcation. In general, before feeding the

HSI into the 2D CNN, it is preprocessed via PCA to select the most informative spectral

bands [104]. Deep belief networks (DBNs) alongside active learning are also employed

by Liu et al. [113] to obtain an effective classiﬁcation framework.

  3D CNN architectures are mostly employed to extract joint spectral-spatial infor-

mation [3, 145]. The 3D deep framework proposed by Hamid et al. [63] takes a 3D

input cube to extract spatial and spectral features simultaneously. Li et al. [105] also

adopted 3D convolutional kernels to integrate spectral and spatial information together.

Using 3D CNNs to extract multi-scale spatiospectral relationships in [68] could add

further improvement to 3D CNN based approaches. However, these 3D convolutional

methods impose high computational costs and parameter size overhead [88, 145]. To

overcome this issue, many recent works aim to utilise two-branch topologies in which

one of the branches is responsible for spectral features extraction, and the other focuses

on spatial information. For instance, in [203] and [198] parallel 1D CNN and 2D CNN

streams were proposed to extract spectral and spatial features, respectively. The results

of two branches are then fused using different strategies like the weighted summation

method [64]. However, combining the results of networks’ spectral and spatial branches

still remains as a challenging unsolved problem.

   In this chapter, different from the above CNN-based approaches, we design a novel

2D CNN topology that can effectively and efﬁciently exploit spectral and spatial hyper-

spectral features simultaneously through only one streamline of information.

5.2.2 CNN Architectures

Over the last decade, various convolutional neural networks (CNNs) such as AlexNet [96],

VGG [159], and GoogleNet [165] have shown outstanding performance in computer vision

and image classiﬁcation [60, 210]. Residual (ResNets) [67] and dense (DenseNets) [77]

aggregations of layer outputs have presented further noticeable progress in the develop-

ment of CNNs’ topologies. Residual links facilitate passing information and gradients

efﬁciently through the network. Dense aggregations offer direct feature re-usage, as

deeper layers have access to the outputs of shallower layers. In fact, they are able to take

advantage of very deep network structures by applying shortcut connections between

stacked layers. In this regard, Paoletti et al. [130] proposed a deep pyramid residual

network (DPyResNet) for HSI classiﬁcation. Likewise, spectral-spatial residual network

(SSRN) [222] took advantages of the residual aggregations’ technique to improve HSI

classiﬁcation performance. Wang et al. [186] proposed an end-to-end fast dense spectral-

spatial convolution (FDSSC) framework for HSI classiﬁcation. The FDSSC framework

uses different convolutional kernel sizes to extract spectral and spatial features sepa-

rately. Kang et al. [93] combined both residual and dense shortcut connections to design

a dual-path network (DPN) for effectively extracting the discriminative features from

the complex scene in HSIs.

   Despite the success of residual and dense skip connections in HSI classiﬁcation, both

aggregation types have drawbacks. As shown in [224],[127], these techniques may cause

information loss and/or parameter over-allocating as the networks get deeper or wider.

Gao et al. [78] used a stochastic residual strategy to alleviate information loss issues

related to the residual networks. More speciﬁcally, since there often exist small numbers

of training samples for HSI classiﬁcation, using generic residual and/or dense topologies

may result in overﬁtting issue and poor generalization capability. In [88] a lightweight

convolutional neural network for hyperspectral image classiﬁcation was presented by

taking aid from spatial-spectral Schroedinger eigenmaps (SSSE) [32] operator, and a

dual-scale convolution procedure (DSC).



5.2.3  Attention Networks

The critical role of a visual attention mechanism in human perception has been shown

through a range of studies [31, 217]. The human vision system efﬁciently and adaptively

focuses on salient areas and suppresses other irrelevant information. Attention mecha-

nism has been widely incorporated in computer vision to improve the efﬁciency of the

   Recently, Hu et al. [72] proposed a lightweight gating mechanism to exploit inter-

Following the idea of SENets attention mechanism, spectral attention (also known as

network (MSDN-SA). More recently, a tow-branch spectral-spatial network was proposed

for hyperspectral image classiﬁcation [64]. However, the two sub-networks have to be

trained separately.

5.3. PROPOSED ATTENTION-BASED LATTICE NETWORK


5.3.1  Joint Spectral-Spatial Attention Mechanism

Capturing joint contextual and spectral information is desired for enhancing the perfor-

mance of the CNN-base HSI classiﬁcation methods [63, 105]. Using 3D convolutional

layers is a common way to exploit both spatial and spectral information. However, 3D

CNNs can cause a signiﬁcant increase in the number of parameters and computation

cost [64]. Recently, Hang et al. [64] proposed an attention-aided 2D CNN framework in

which a spectral attention sub-network and a spatial sub-network are responsible for

extracting spectral and spatial features, respectively. Unlike this strategy, we leverage

joint spectral and spatial attention mechanisms into a sequential design of 2D convo-

lutional elements. The idea behind the new joint spectral-spatial attention module is

illustrated in Figure 5.2. The input 3D tensor is reﬁned by applying two consecutive

point-wise spectral and spatial attention modules, respectively.

    Typically, all channel-wise features are treated equally by CNN-based HSI classi-

ﬁcation networks [63, 105, 130]. This policy hinders the network’s ability to deal with

different types of spectral information. Hence, considering the inter-dependencies among

bands (channels) as a spectral attention mechanism can achieve better classiﬁcation

performance [72, 184]. Moreover, it is well-known that utilizing contextual information

is crucial to know which spatial locations should be focused on [194]. In this chapter,

both spectral and spatial axes of attention are exploited with a simple yet effective joint

spectral-spatial attention (JSS) module. As shown in Figure 5.2, JSS attention module
ρJSS reﬁnes a given intermediate feature map x ∈Rc×h×w sequentially on its spectral
bands and spatial locations, respectively. The re-calibrated feature map ¯x is computed

as:

                                                           ¯x = ρJSS(x) = ρs(ρpw(x)),                               (5.1)

where ρs(.) and ρpw(.) represent spatial and point-wise spectral attention modules

respectively.

5.3.1.2  Point-wise Spectral Attention

Using squeeze and excitation operations [73] is a common way to adopt a spectrally

(channel-wise) attention mechanism. To this end, they generally apply a global pooling

operator (e.g. average) to shrink the given c feature maps through their spatial dimen-
sions h × w. Despite the advantage of these methods, the global pooled information is

not the optimal features to infer accurate channel attention [194]. Furthermore, since

the ﬁnal goal is pixel-wise classiﬁcation of HSI, global information may impact the

performance. To address this shortcoming, we remove the squeezing function (global

pooling) and adopt a point-wise excitation mechanism to fully capture spectral depen-

dencies for every pixel. The structure of the point-wise spectral attention module is

illustrated in Figure 5.3 (b). The excitation operator acts as a gating mechanism to learn

nonlinear synergies between channels alongside a non-mutually-exclusive relationship

for every spatial location. Here, we adopt the point-wise spectral gating mechanism by

forming a bottleneck with two fully connected (FC) layers. The ﬁrst FC layer followed by

ReLU [122] non-linearity (δ) reduces the spectrum dimension with ratio r (here, we set
r = 16) and then an up-sampling FC layer followed by sigmoid activation (σ) returns the

input spectral dimension (c). Therefore, the ﬁnal point-wise spectral attention map Mpc

can be formalized as:

                         Mpw(i, j) = σ(fU(δ(fD(x(i, j))))),                          (5.4)
where x(i, j) ∈Rc×1×1 refers to the spectral feature vector at position (i, j). fD and fU rep-

resent the shared FC layers for channel reduction and up-sampling operators respectively.

Finally, reﬁned input cube is adaptively formed by Mpw as:

                                ρpw(x) = Mpw ⊗x,                                  (5.5)

where ⊗represents element-wise multiplication operator.

The input to a convolutional unit in the lattice, xld, is the dense aggregation of the

5.3.6  Implementation Details

In this work, we set the convolutional unit output size at each level to Cl = Cl−1 +32,
where C1 = 64 is the output size at l = 1. This setting ensures that a reduced number of

parameters are used for feature re-usage. The maximum depth and levels of the lattice
block are set to D = 3 and L = 3, respectively. Concerning the spatial size of the input 3D
cube (p × p), patches with the resolution of 9×9 are used.

  We use stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for the training of the proposed models.

In particular, we adopt Adam optimizer [94] with default hyperparameters. All models

are trained for 200 epochs with a mini-batch size of 128 and an initial learning rate
of 0.001, which is decayed to 10−6 by adopting the cosine annealing technique [115]. A

single NVIDIA Geforce Titan RTX GPU card is used to carry out all experiments. All

experiments are repeated ten times, and mean values are reported to avoid the inﬂuence

of weight initialization and randomness of data sampling.




5.4  Experimental Results and Discussion


The effectiveness of the proposed ALN for HSI classiﬁcation is evaluated across three

well-known benchmark hyperspectral datasets. Further, we use overall accuracy (OA),

average accuracy (AA), and kappa (κ) statistics to evaluate the performance. Speciﬁcally,

OA is deﬁned as the ratio of correctly classiﬁed samples among the total test samples.

AA represents the average of class-wise accuracy, and κ measures a strong mutual

agreement between the given ground truth and the classiﬁcation map generated by the

model.

5.5  Conclusion


In this chapter, we present a novel attention-based lattice network (ALN) for hyper-

spectral image classiﬁcation. Unlike other CNNs that use either residual or dense

aggregations, ALN takes advantage of both aggregation types more efﬁciently and

effectively. Moreover, ALN utilizes a unique point-wise spectral schema alongside spa-

tial attention mechanisms to effectively exploit inter-dependencies among spectral and

spatial features. These properties enable ALN to achieve a superior performance and

excellent efﬁciency in terms of model complexity than 2D/3D-CNN based benchmarks in

HSI classiﬁcation. We further verify the effectiveness of each component of the proposed

ALN via an extensive ablation study.
